READING

**The numbers at face value**

MORVEDD offers GBP 302,400 a year of incremental revenue over SALTGRAVE, on a three-year horizon that totals GBP 907,200. The GBP 96,000 capital cost pays back in roughly 3.8 months of incremental income. Those are real gains and the jigs remain Gallowfield's property regardless. Viewed as a pure capital-allocation question, MORVEDD looks compelling.

The problem is that the numbers are not the whole picture.

---

**What the contract actually is**

The draft gives either side the right to exit on six months' notice on a change of control. On the surface this is standard boilerplate. In context it is the most important clause in the document.

Vennerdale bought Thurlmere in 2025 — last year. They are a demonstrated acquirer, actively reshaping their portfolio. The change-of-control clause would be triggered not by the 2025 deal (that is already done and baked in) but by any further corporate event: Vennerdale being sold, merged, or demerged; Thurlmere being transferred to a different Vennerdale vehicle; a financial restructuring that technically passes control. In an active acquirer's hands, those events are not remote tail risks. They are plausible within a three-year window.

What Gallowfield is actually being offered, therefore, is not a three-year contract. It is a contract that can become a six-month contract at any point Vennerdale's corporate life becomes eventful. The headline GBP 907,200 is not locked in; it is conditional on Vennerdale's stability.

---

**The concentration problem under MORVEDD**

At present no single customer exceeds 44%. Under MORVEDD, Thurlmere moves to roughly 62% of a slightly larger revenue base. That is not just high concentration; it is high concentration in a customer whose ultimate controller has unknown intentions and an exit mechanism ready to hand.

Nineteen employees, GBP 2.1m turnover, one untouched bank facility: this is not a business that absorbs a 60%-customer departure in stride. If Thurlmere exits on six months' notice after year one, Gallowfield finds itself with: Marchgate (still uncontracted), no Ostrey, two jigs equipped with a dedicated liquor circuit whose next use is unclear, and revenues roughly halved. The bank facility would be drawn heavily and staff decisions would follow quickly.

The payback arithmetic looks good — the GBP 96,000 is recovered in under four months — but payback on the equipment is not the real exposure. The real exposure is operational: the business remade around a 62% customer who can leave after six months on grounds outside Gallowfield's control.

---

**What is being permanently given up**

Ostrey have been on the book for twenty-two years. They are offering a committed three-year contract at a modest premium to the average rate. Their offer stands until 28 November 2026, several weeks after the Thurlmere deadline, so Gallowfield can resolve Thurlmere first and still accept Ostrey.

If MORVEDD is taken, Ostrey are released and the relationship is effectively over. A competitor dyeworks will pick them up. A 22-year customer relationship, once severed to make room for a corporate buyer, does not come back. SALTGRAVE + Ostrey contract produces a book with three names, the largest at 44%, with the smallest secured for three years — a materially more resilient base than either course gives on its own.

---

**The Marchgate exposure that neither course removes**

Both courses leave Marchgate — the largest customer, 44% of revenue — without a contract. This is a live vulnerability in either scenario. SALTGRAVE does not fix it; but SALTGRAVE does not worsen it either. Under MORVEDD, if Marchgate also departed, the business would have only Thurlmere, whose stability is itself dependent on Vennerdale. Under SALTGRAVE with Ostrey contracted, losing Marchgate is severe but not fatal: Thurlmere (31%) and Ostrey (25%) together still represent over half of current revenue, and all four jigs remain available to seek replacement volume. The residual base is more navigable.

Whatever course is chosen, securing a formal commitment from Marchgate should be the next action after the Thurlmere and Ostrey deadlines are resolved.

---

**Could Thurlmere leave without a new contract anyway?**

If Gallowfield declines MORVEDD, Thurlmere needs dedicated capacity and will find another dyeworks to give it. Their current 31% of Gallowfield's book may reduce or disappear. That loss is real, not trivial. But it is a loss from a known baseline, suffered once. MORVEDD's failure mode — 62% of revenue on six months' notice, Ostrey gone, infrastructure partly committed — is larger in magnitude and harder to recover from.

---

**Balancing the case**

The argument for MORVEDD is genuine: fast payback, higher margin, three-year commitment (if it holds), and a substantial annual premium. It is not a frivolous course.

The argument against rests on three compounding factors, none of which alone is decisive, but which together tip the balance:

1. The change-of-control clause converts the three-year commitment into a rolling six-month commitment whenever Vennerdale's corporate life moves — and Vennerdale has already shown it moves.
2. The post-MORVEDD concentration (62%) in that fragile commitment is too high for a nineteen-person business with a single bank facility.
3. The price of accepting those two risks is the permanent, unrecoverable loss of a 22-year customer who is actively offering security.

SALTGRAVE with the Ostrey contract accepted is the sounder course.

---

CALL
SALTGRAVE

GROUNDS
The change-of-control clause reduces Thurlmere's three-year contract to a rolling six-month option in the hands of a group that made one acquisition in 2025 and may make another within the contract term, and accepting 62% concentration on that basis while permanently surrendering a 22-year contracted customer is a risk disproportionate to the GBP 302,400 annual premium.
